name: Calendula extract
lead: Calendula extract is a preparation from the flowers of Calendula officinalis, used in topical skincare and traditional wound-care products. Laboratory studies have reported anti-inflammatory properties for flower extracts,[4] and human and animal studies have examined it mainly for wound healing.[1]

A 2019 systematic review of calendula extract as a single treatment for wound healing covered 14 studies, 7 animal experiments and 7 clinical trials.[1] No published trial listed here has tested it for cosmetic appearance goals such as acne or skin aging.

paras: Calendula extract appears in topical wound-care and skincare products. Studies have also examined it in a mouthwash for radiation-induced oral mucositis.[2] One study measured effects of calendula extract on mechanical parameters of human skin.[5]

Laboratory work includes a rodent study reporting that oral flower extract reduced induced paw swelling,[4] and in vitro work on a laser-activated extract reporting cytotoxic and lymphocyte-activating effects.[3] These findings come from animal or cell models and are not evidence of appearance benefit in people. Formulation research has examined hydrogels and nanoparticles for delivery.[6]

The 2019 systematic review included seven clinical trials of calendula extract for wound healing.[1] In a randomized study of 40 head-and-neck cancer patients, a 2% calendula mouthwash was compared with placebo for radiation-induced oropharyngeal mucositis.[2] A study of calendula extract on mechanical parameters of human skin has also been published.[5] Trials focused on cosmetic skin appearance were not found among the sources reviewed.

card.summary: Marigold flower extract used in soothing skincare; studied for wound healing, with no appearance-specific trials found.
card.note: Research is mainly on wound healing and animal or lab models.

quick.overview:
Calendula extract comes from pot marigold flowers and is used in topical products for soothing skin.

Research has examined wound healing and oral mucositis, plus animal and lab work on inflammation; appearance-specific trials were not found.
quick.mechanism: Laboratory studies report anti-inflammatory activity of flower extracts; the mechanism in human skin is not established in the sources reviewed.[4]
quick.risks: The sources reviewed do not describe significant adverse effects of topical use; safety data are limited to the small studies cited.
